list.listitem: Preterm labor (PTL) is diagnosed clinically based on cervical dilation, effacement or both in the presence of regular uterine contractions or contractions and cervical dilation of at least 2 cm at initial presentation.C

Cervical ultrasonography is recommended in women with suspected PTL for its negative predictive value. Abdominal ultrasound to assess placental location, amniotic fluid volume, estimated fetal weight and presentation, and fetal wellbeing is also recommended. B

In women with suspected PTL, a sterile speculum examination is recommended to assess rupture of membranes (pooled fluid) if the patient has not had intercourse or vaginal bleeding in the last 24 hours, pH, ferning (prepare slide), infection (cultures for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and Group B streptococcus), and to obtain a swab for fetal fibronectin. C

With respect to prevention efforts among high-risk women, data are positive for omega-3 supplements, conflicting for use of progestins with a recent meta-analysis showing positive results for at-risk women using vaginal progesterone, and negative for most other interventions including cervical length monitoring. B
Prophylactic vaginal progesterone therapy should be considered for women at high-risk of preterm birth who have a short cervix (<15 mm at 22-26 weeks' gestation). B

The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ACOG) recommends beta-adrenergic agonist therapy, calcium channel blockers (CCBs), or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to manage PTL. A Cochrane authors and another meta-analysis found CCBs to be more effective than beta-mimetics with fewer adverse effects. A

Tocolytic drugs may prolong pregnancy for 2 to 7 days, which can allow for administration of steroids to improve fetal lung maturity and the consideration of maternal transport to a tertiary care facility. A Maintenance tocolytics and progestins are ineffective. A
Bed rest, hydration, pelvic rest, and antibiotics do not appear to improve the rate of preterm birth and should not be routinely recommended. B

A single dose of antenatal corticosteroids should be given to at risk of preterm birth who are between 24- and 34-weeks gestation. A Repeat doses appear useful for women still at risk of preterm birth 7 or more days after an initial dose to reduce the occurrence and severity of neonatal lung disease and serious morbidity. BA

Consideration should be given to antenatal magnesium sulphate administration for fetal neuroprotection for women with imminent preterm birth at 24 to 29 + 6 weeks of pregnancy, with consideration in women between 30 and 33 + 6 weeks, although supporting data are limited. B
For women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes, a policy of expectant management with careful monitoring is associated with better outcomes for the mother and baby than immediate delivery. A

background.definition: Preterm labor (PTL) is defined as regular contractions associated with cervical change before the completion of 37 weeks of gestation.

list.listitem: Since 1970, the incidence of preterm deliveries in developed countries increased from 9% to 11%. In 2013, the preterm birth rate in the United States declined to 11.4%, the lowest rate since 1997; this is possibly due in part to successful interventions.
After 2014, however, rates of preterm births rose for three consecutive years and in 2017 was 9% among white women and 14% among Africa American women (CDC).
Among young women ages 15 to 19 years, the preterm birth rate decreased from 10.41% in 2007 to 9.54% of live births in 2014 or 24.2/1000 females.
In 2019 according to a CDC report, the preterm birth rate rose to 9.3% for whites and 10% for Hispanics compared to 14.4% for African Americans.
More than 470,000 babies are born preterm every year in the United States.

Based on a systematic review, among women presenting with symptoms of PTL at <35 weeks' gestation, 16.2% will deliver preterm. For those presenting at <37 weeks' gestation, 30.2% will deliver preterm.
Preterm premature rupture of membranes occurs in approximately 3% of all pregnancies in the U.S.
Preterm birth accounts for 35% of all U.S. health care spending for infants and 10% of all such spending for children.
The estimated annual societal cost of preterm birth in the U.S. in 2005 was at least $26.2 billion or more than $51,000 per preterm infant.

While the incidence of death and long-term disability is relatively low in those born after 32 weeks, this group comprises over 80% of all preterm deliveries and, therefore, has a significant impact on public health and health care costs.
Preterm birth is responsible for 70% of all neonatal deaths, 36% of infant deaths and 25% to 50% of cases of long-term neurologic impairment in children.
Of infants born before 37 weeks gestation, approximately 8.3% will be low birthweight.
Complications of prematurity are responsible for more than 60% of perinatal morbidity and mortality.
Having a preterm birth at <34 weeks of gestation increases the risk of a subsequent stillbirth (pooled OR 2.98; 95% CI, 2.05-4.34).

Infection (amniotic or cervicovaginal). In pregnant women infected with coronavirus disease-19, rates of PTL are reported in 29.7% based on 44 case series and 16% (95% CI, 11%-21%) based on data obtained from 16 observational studies.
Decidual hemorrhage (abruption).
Mechanical factors (uterine overdistention or cervical incompetence).
Iatrogenic (induced for medical conditions and/or pregnancy complications).
Hormonal changes (fetal and/or maternal stress).

There appears to be a relatively low heritability of gestational age and spontaneous preterm birth in the general population. However, recent literature suggests there may be a genetic component to preterm birth. Familial history of PTL occurs almost 15% to 40% more in families with a maternal or sibling with a history of preterm labor.
Preterm labor is largely idiopathic and causes are multifactorial.
The most common pathway for urogenital pathogens to cause PTL is the ascending route.

Short cervical length between 14 and 28 weeks
Previous surgical abortion (medical abortion did not increase risk)
Previous abortion (more than one vs. none)
Use of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (preterm birth)

list.listitem: Screening for risk of PTL by means other than historic risk factors is not beneficial in the general obstetric population. B
Data do not support the use of salivary estriol, home uterine activity monitoring (HUAM), or bacterial vaginosis screening as strategies to identify or prevent preterm birth. A
Use of vaginal progesterone in at-risk women likely reduces both early and late preterm birth, although data are conflicting. B

Prophylactic therapy including tocolytic drugs, bed rest, hydration, and sedation, in asymptomatic women at increased risk for preterm delivery is not effective. A Progesterone could be considered in women with prior preterm birth. B

The USPSTF recommends against screening for bacterial vaginosis (BV) in asymptomatic pregnant women at low risk for preterm birth and concluded that evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for BV in asymptomatic pregnant women at high risk.
In one large trial, routine screening of women for vaginal infections decreased the risk of preterm delivery (number needed to screen and treat = 44).

listitem.strong: Cervical assessment and uterine activity monitoring

list.listitem: Based on two trials, there is no evidence to support the use of repeat digital cervical assessment in pregnancy to reduce the prevalence of preterm birth.
Screening for cervical length with second-trimester transvaginal ultrasound is not associated with improved outcomes in women carrying twins. B

In a RCT of 125 women with twin pregnancies, use of routine transvaginal cervical length ultrasound examinations did not reduce rates of delivery prior to 35 weeks' gestation (27.4% vs. 28.6% for control subjects).

Ultrasound cervical elastography may improve prediction of preterm delivery. Authors of a meta-analysis of seven studies with 1448 low-risk or at-risk pregnant women found cervical elastography, which measures cervical stiffness, performed better than measuring cervical length for predicting preterm delivery with an area under the curve of 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.93) vs. 0.60 (95% CI, 0.56-0.64).
HUAM is not recommended as a screening method for PTL and birth in high-risk pregnancies.

The USPSTF recommends against screening for BV in asymptomatic pregnant women at low-risk for preterm birth and concluded that evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for BV in asymptomatic pregnant women at high risk.

In a large RCT of 4155 women, screening and treating bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas vaginalis, or candidiasis in the early second trimester of pregnancy reduced the number of preterm births (before 37 weeks) compared to control women (3% vs. 5.3%); absolute risk reduction 2.3% (95% CI, 1.2%-3.6%), number needed to screen and treat = 44.

Based on a Cochrane review of 15 good-quality RCTs, it was unclear whether screening and treatment of pregnant women for BV would prevent preterm birth and its consequences; there was some evidence that treatment before 20 weeks' gestation reduced preterm birth.

In the most recent RCT using clindamycin for treating BV prior to 14 weeks gestation, there were no differences in preterm births among 2869 women with low-risk pregnancies (1.2% vs. 1.0% for placebo). In a subtrial of 236 high-risk women, there was no significant difference in preterm birth rate between women randomized to a single course vs. triple course of clindamycin (6% vs. 4.4%, respectively).

In an RCT of 1727 pregnant women conducted in a low-resource setting in India, treating women with an elevated vaginal pH with clindamycin vs. placebo was also not effective (preterm birth <34 weeks gestation 4.8% vs. 4.6%).

Treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in women with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy did not reduce the proportion of women with pyelonephritis, preterm birth, or both (2.5% and 2.9%) in a RCT embedded within a cohort study; in fact, asymptomatic bacteriuria was not associated with preterm birth but was associated with a small risk of pyelonephritis (2.4% vs. 0.6% among asymptomatic bacteriuria-negative women).

In one large RCT of 1082 women, treating for periodontal disease (15% of the total population) during pregnancy vs. post-partum did not reduce the risk of preterm birth (9.7% vs. 9.3% preterm birth rate, respectively).
Preconception low-dose aspirin was not associated with a reduced rate of preterm birth.

Use of vitamin C/E supplementation starting at 9 to 16 weeks in low-risk nulliparous women with singleton gestations was effective in preventing preterm birth among smokers (RR 0.76; 95% CI, 0.58-0.99) but not in nonsmokers (RR 1.03; 95% CI, 0.90-1.17); findings were similar for prevention of placental abruption.
In women with maternal thyroid autoantibodies, levothyroxine was shown in one study to decrease preterm birth.

In another RCT of 366 women with subclinical hypothyroidism who were negative for thyroid peroxidase antibodies, use of levothyroxine vs. placebo was of no benefit in reducing preterm birth using a TSH cutoff of 2.5 mIU/L. The authors found a lower rate of preterm birth posthoc using a TSH cutoff of 4.0 mIU/L (RR: 0.38; 95% CI, 0.15-0.98).

In an RCT conducted in 7 community sites within 6 resource-poor countries with 11,558 nulliparous women with singleton gestations who delivered at 20 0/7 weeks' gestation or later, those randomized to 81 mg daily aspirin had fewer births before 37 0/7 weeks' compared to the placebo group (11.6% vs. 13.1%, respectively; RR 0.89; 95% CI, 0.81-0.98; number needed to treat = 66; 37-308).
Caffeine intake does not appear to be a risk factor for preterm birth.
Aerobic exercise is also not a risk factor for preterm birth.

Investigators in one RCT found a diet rich in fish and low in other animal fats decreased preterm birth among high-risk women (0.7% vs. 7.4%; NNT = 15).In another report of six European trials, fish oil reduced the incidence of recurrent preterm delivery but not the occurrence of low birth weight.
There is no evidence that use of prophylactic oral betamimetics, probiotics, or bedrest prevents preterm birth in women at high risk of PTL.
There is insufficient evidence to support or refute use of oral betamimetics for preventing preterm birth in women with a twin pregnancy; quality of evidence is generally poor.

Data on use of progestins for prevention of preterm delivery is conflicting. NICE recommends intervention for women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth or mid-trimester loss between 16 and 34 weeks' gestation AND a cervical length <25 mm with either prophylactic vaginal progesterone or prophylactic cervical cerclage. Women with twin pregnancy and a short cervix may also benefit.

At-risk women based on history (e.g., prior preterm birth). Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs found progestational agents (intramuscular or vaginal) given to high-risk women in the second trimester reduced the risk of preterm delivery (NNT = 6).Authors of a Cochrane review of 11 RCTs found progesterone beneficial in preventing preterm birth for women with a previous history of preterm birth (4 trials; 1255 women; RR 0.80; 95% CI, 0.70-0.92). A single study found a reduction in preterm birth for women with a short cervix, but not for women with multiple gestation or other risk factors.

Authors of a recent meta-analysis of 40 RCTs found use of vaginal progesterone in at-risk women reduced both early and late preterm birth (OR 0.43; 95% credibility interval [CrI], 0.20-0.81 and OR 0.51; 95% CrI, 0.34-0.74) and neonatal death (OR 0.41; 95% CrI, 0.20-0.83).

However, the two most recent RCTs of vaginal progesterone given to women at high risk of preterm birth were negative. The first, with 618 high-risk women (previous preterm birth or cervical length ≤25 mm or positive fetal fibronectin test combined with other clinical risk factors) vs. 610 receiving placebo, did not demonstrate differences in obstetric or neonatal outcomes. In an Australian study of 787 pregnant women with a history of preterm birth at less than 37 weeks' were randomized to daily treatment with vaginal progesterone 100 mg daily or placebo starting at 20 weeks' gestation. Cervical length was not considered in this study. Preterm birth rates were similar in both groups: 38.2% vs. 38.7%.

In the largest, well-designed RCT including 1708 women with prior preterm birth from 93 centers across 9 countries, use of 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate did not decrease recurrent preterm birth or neonatal morbidity.

In an open-label RCT of 247 women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth or cervical length <25 mm, there was no difference in preterm birth between women randomized to vaginal vs. intramuscular progesterone (22.7 vs. 25.8%, respectively).

Arrested PTL. Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs, including 426 women, found no benefit of 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate maintenance tocolysis for arrested PTL on preterm birth at <37 weeks (42% vs. 51%) or <34 weeks (25% vs. 34%) compared to controls. However, in a more recent meta-analysis cited above, among women with a previous preterm birth, 17α-hydroxyprogesterone caproate reduced preterm birth at <37 weeks (OR 0.53; 95% CrI, 0.27-0.95) and neonatal death (OR 0.39; 95% CI, 0.16-0.95).

Short cervix. Women at high-risk with a short cervix (<15 mm at 22-26 weeks' gestation) should be considered for use of prophylactic progesterone therapy (progesterone 200 mg daily vaginally). However, in an RCT of 105 women with a short cervix who were at high risk for preterm birth, 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate given at 500 mg IM weekly until 36 weeks was NOT effective in prolonging pregnancy; preterm delivery at <37 weeks occurred in 45% vs. 44% of control women.

Similar results were demonstrated in an RCT of 80 low-risk women with a short cervix (30 mm or less; found in 1.8% of the 20,234 women screened) in which vaginal progesterone was not effective in reducing adverse neonatal outcome and preterm birth. The study was likely underpowered.

In the most recent meta-analysis of 5 RCTs with 974 women with a short cervix <25 mm, vaginal progesterone reduced the risk of preterm birth <33 weeks gestation (RR 0.62; 95% CI, 0.47-0.81). Maternal and infant adverse events did not differ between groups.

Combined use of vaginal progesterone with a cervical pessary in asymptomatic women with a singleton gestation and a mid-trimester sonographic short cervix was not more effective for preventing preterm birth than vaginal progesterone alone based on a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs with 820 participants.

Pregnancy with twins. Prophylactic treatment with 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate for women with twin pregnancy was also NOT useful for either prolonging gestation or reducing neonatal morbidity. In another RCT of 380 women with twin pregnancies, vaginal progesterone administration did not prevent preterm delivery or reduce neonatal morbidity or death. However, in the most recent trial of 250 women with twin pregnancy and sonographic evidence of a short cervix (20-25 mm), vaginal progesterone administration starting at 20 to 24 weeks' gestation was effective in reducing the incidence of PTL and neonatal morbidity.
Prophylactic antibiotics should not be given to women in PTL without signs of infection; there is no benefit on neonatal outcomes and there is evidence of potential harm.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of antenatal magnesium sulfate as a neuroprotective agent for the preterm fetus. Magnesium sulfate given to pregnant women at imminent risk of birth before 30 weeks' gestation was not associated with neurological, cognitive, behavioral, growth, or functional outcomes in their children at school age, based on a follow-up study of 669 children (77% of survivors).
Administration of vitamin K or phenobarbital prior to preterm birth did not prevent neonatal periventricular hemorrhage.

In a meta-analysis with two RCT’s, omega-3 supplementation during pregnancy did not prevent recurrent preterm birth in asymptomatic singleton gestations. Authors of a Cochrane review, however, found high-quality evidence that omega-3 supplementation primarily for high-risk women was effective for preventing preterm birth prior to 37 weeks (13.4% vs. 11.9%; risk ratio [RR] 0.89; 95% CI, 0.81-0.97; 26 RCTs, 10,304 participants) and early preterm birth (4.6% vs. 2.7%; RR 0.58; 95% CI, 0.44-0.77; 9 RCTs, 5204 participants).

Authors of a Cochrane review of a single trial including 385 pregnant women with a short cervix of 25 mm or less who were between 18 to 22 weeks of pregnancy found benefit of a cervical pessary in reducing preterm birth (22% vs. 59% in women undergoing expectant management; risk ratio 0.36; 95% CI, 0.27-0.49).

In a RCT of 932 women with singleton pregnancies who had a cervical length of 25 mm or less at 20 to 24 weeks 6 days of gestation, there was no significant difference between the pessary group and the control group in the rate of spontaneous delivery before 34 weeks or adverse neonatal outcomes.

Although routine treatment with a cervical pessary did not reduce the rate of spontaneous early preterm birth among unselected women with twins, it was effective in reducing preterm birth among women with twin gestation and a short cervix (11/68 [16.2%] vs. 26/66 [39.4%]). There were no differences in neonatal outcomes between groups in the latter study. In the most recent RCT of 503 women with twin pregnancy and cervical length ≤35 mm, there was no difference in preterm birth before 34 weeks gestation between those randomized to pessary vs. standard care alone (18.4% vs. 20.6%, respectively).

Among 357 women who had experienced an episode of threatened preterm labor and had a short cervix (≤25 mm at 240-296 weeks; ≤15 mm at 300-336 weeks), those randomized to use of a cervical pessary had similar rates of preterm birth at <34 weeks but fewer preterm births at <37 weeks gestation (14.7% vs. 25.1%). In addition, women randomized to the pessary had a lower preterm premature rupture of membranes rate (2.3% vs. 8.0%) and less frequently required readmission for new threatened preterm labor episodes (4.5% vs. 20.0%). There were no differences in maternal or neonatal morbidity and mortality.

PTL is a clinical diagnosis based on cervical dilation, effacement or both in the presence of regular uterine contractions or contractions and cervical dilation of at least 2 cm at initial presentation before 37 weeks gestation. C
Fetal fibronectin (fFN) testing may be useful for women with symptoms of PTL to identify those with negative values and a reduced risk of preterm birth. B

Ultrasonography to determine cervical length, fFN testing, or a combination of both may be useful in determining women at high risk for PTL. However, their greatest value is when negative (negative predictive value) given the lack of proven treatment options to prevent preterm birth. B

NICE recommends consideration of transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length to determine likelihood of birth within 48 hours for women who are 30 or more weeks' gestation and in suspected PTL. If cervical length is >15 mm, the woman is unlikely to be in preterm labor.

Differential.Differential_Features: Regular uterine contractions without cervical change
Urinalysis with leukocytes and either blood, bacteria, nitrites; positive culture; no cervical change
Wet prep positive for trichomonas, gonorrhea, chlamydia or bacterial vaginosis (BV); no cervical change

list.listitem: Preterm labor (PTL) is diagnosed clinically based on cervical dilation, effacement or both in the presence of regular uterine contractions or contractions and cervical dilation of at least 2 cm at initial presentation prior to 37 weeks gestation.

Patients present with signs and symptoms of PTL including painful or painless uterine contractions, pelvic pressure, menstrual-like cramps, watery vaginal discharge, low back pain, and/or abdominal and pelvic symptoms that last longer than an hour in the second half of pregnancy.
Maternal perception of symptoms, however, has a low predictive value for PTL.

General physical examination includes blood pressure (preeclampsia), temperature (maternal infection, chorioamnionitis), external fetal heart rate monitor (fetal demise) and contraction monitor (true vs. false labor).

A sterile speculum examination is recommended to assess rupture of membranes (pooled fluid) if the patient has not had intercourse or vaginal bleeding in the last 24 hours, pH, ferning (prepare slide), infection (cultures for gonorrhea, chlamydia, and Group B streptococcus), and to obtain a swab for fetal fibronectin.
A cervical examination is completed to assess cervical dilation; dilation >3 cm most likely indicates PTL. Women with cervical dilation <2 cm should be observed for 2 hours and the cervix reexamined.

fFN is an extracellular matrix protein present at the decidual-chorionic interface. Disruption of this interface due to subclinical infection or inflammation, abruption, or uterine contractions releases fFN into cervicovaginal secretions, which is the basis for its use as a marker for predicting spontaneous preterm birth.

Qualitative fFN results are reported as positive or negative. A positive fFN test refers to a fFN concentration ≥50 ng/mL in cervicovaginal fluid between 22 + 0 and 34 + 6 weeks of gestation in women with intact membranes, cervical dilation <3 cm, and no gross vaginal bleeding.

Authors of systematic reviews claim that the cervicovaginal fetal fibronectin (FFN) is accurate in predicting spontaneous preterm birth within 7 to 10 days of testing among women with symptoms of PTL before cervical dilation. However, the negative likelihood ratio and hence negative predictive value for prediction of preterm birth <34 weeks or <37 weeks (0.25-0.78) is only modest. Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 trials including 546 women with singleton gestations and symptoms of PTL found no association between fFN testing and prevention of preterm birth or improvement in perinatal outcome; testing was associated with higher costs. This test is recommended by ACOG and ICSI.

Alternative risk thresholds can improve accuracy of fFN for defining risk of spontaneous preterm birth, particularly for asymptomatic women with a short cervix. In one study, women with a fFN <10 ng/mL has a rate of preterm birth at <34 weeks of 2.7%. Among women with a short cervix, 9.5% delivered prematurely with a fFN <10 ng/mL compared with 55.1% of women whose fFN level was >200 ng/mL.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 studies of quantitative FFN found pooled sensitivities for diagnosis of spontaneous PTL at <34 weeks for thresholds of 10, 50, 200, and 500 ng/ml of 0.78, 0.56, 0.33, and 0.11, respectively and pooled specificities of 0.63, 0.84, 0.96, and 0.99, respectively.
False-positive results can occur due to ejaculate from coitus within the previous 24 hours, a grossly bloody specimen, or digital cervical examination.

Observational studies have shown that maternal levels of serum estradiol and salivary estriol increase before the onset of spontaneous term and PTL. Trials to date have not supported use of salivary estriol to identify or prevent PTL.
Higher levels of a serum protein serpin B7 were associated with a shorter interval to delivery and, in samples from 28 to 2 weeks, were associated with a lower gestational age at delivery.

Cervical ultrasonography is recommended by ACOG, ICSI, and ACR in women with suspected PTL. Its clinical usefulness is in its negative predictive value given the lack of proven treatment options to prevent preterm birth.

A systematic review suggests that cervical length less than or equal to 30 mm on transvaginal ultrasound will identify 80% to 100% of women who will have a preterm birth. A cohort study found cervical length <30 mm had a positive predictive value of 46% and 63% and a negative predictive value of 90% and 43% for singleton and twin pregnancies respectively.In another study of women with prior preterm birth, a cervical length <25 mm predicted birth at less than 35 weeks but not cervical lengths ≥25 mm.

In a meta-analysis of studies of women carrying twins, cervical length less than or equal to 20 mm at 20 to 24 weeks' gestation was the most accurate in predicting preterm birth less than 32 and less than 34 weeks' gestation (positive and negative likelihood ratios of 10.1 and 9.0, and 0.64 and 0.74, respectively); a cervical length less than or equal to 25 mm at 20 to 24 weeks' gestation was also useful for predicting preterm birth less than 28 weeks' gestation (pooled LR+ 9.6).
However, monthly measurement of cervical length via ultrasound and digital exam in women with twin pregnancy and no history of PTL was not useful for reducing preterm birth.

listitem.strong: Cervical length plus fFN or other factors

list.listitem: Combination cervcal length and fFN may be useful for predicting preterm birth in women presenting with symptomatic uterine contractions but the positive predictive value was only 49.4% in one systematic review. In one cohort study of 665 women with symptoms of PTL and intact membranes, those with a cervical length of at least 30 mm or with a cervical length between 15 and 30 mm AND a negative fFN were at low risk (less than 5%) of spontaneous delivery within 7 days.

In another study, the combination of serum interleukin-10 levels, serum RANTES levels and cervical length predicted spontaneous preterm delivery within 7 days with an area under the ROC curve of 0.88. Another model, after validation, combined maternal characteristics (age, race, educational level, and income), obstetrical history (prior preterm birth, parity), gestational age at presentation and cervical factors (length and glandular area present) resulting in an area under the curve of 0.90 for women with preterm contractions and intact membranes.

Cervical length plus amniotic fluid index may be helpful in predicting delivery latency for women with premature rupture of membranes (PPROM). In one study of 106 women with singleton pregnancies and PPROM between 23 and 33 weeks, cervical length ≤2 cm and an AFI ≤5 cm predicted delivery within 7 days, although having a combination of low TVCL and low AFI did not increase the predictive value. Only 3 of 27 women (11%) with neither characteristic delivered within 7 days.
Home uterine activity monitoring (HUAM) has been proposed as a method for predicting PTL. However, data are insufficient to support a benefit from HUAM in preventing preterm.
Transabdominal ultrasound examination for placental location, amniotic fluid volume, estimated fetal weight and presentation, and fetal well being is recommended.

PTL is a clinical diagnosis based on cervical dilation and effacement (3 cm dilation, 80% effacement) in the presence of regular uterine contractions or contractions plus rupture of membranes or contractions plus cervical change during observation before 37 weeks gestation.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to the woman with PTL.

ACOG provides a practice guideline for management of pregnant women with COVID-19. Pregnant women admitted with suspected COVID-19 or who develop symptoms suggestive of COVID-19 during admission should be prioritized for testing. Additional testing strategies may be appropriate, such as universal testing.

To date, studies have found no evidence of the virus in breastmilk or amniotic fluid. However, ACOG recommends that infants born to women with known COVID-19 at the time of delivery should be considered infants with suspected COVID-19, tested, and isolated from other healthy infants.

A case report and case series of 1 and 38 births, respectively, found no evidence of infection by PCR in the infants born to mothers with COVID-19. Vertical transmission of infection therefore seems unlikely. In the systematic review noted above, vertical transmission was suspected in only 4 cases.
WHO interim guidance recommends that mother and infant be allowed to remain together and have skin to skin contact, regardless of whether they or their infant have COVID-19 infection.

listitem.strong: Comfort care for very preterm infant

list.listitem: For infants born very preterm (22-25 weeks' gestation), authors of a systematic review of 31 guidelines from highly-developed countries found 21 (68%) supported comfort care at 22 weeks' gestation and 20 (65%) supported active care at 25 weeks' gestation.

Authors of a systematic review of guidelines for PTL from 16 developers current from 2013 found consistent recommendations for cervical length screening for high-risk women; short-term tocolysis; steroids for fetal lung maturation; and magnesium sulphate for fetal neuroprotection.

ACOG recommends beta-adrenergic agonist therapy, CCBs, or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to manage PTL; they offer no recommendation for a "first-line" tocolytic drug to manage PTL. Clinical circumstances and physician preferences should dictate treatment. A Authors of a Cochrane review and another meta-analysis, however, found CCBs more effective than beta-mimetics with fewer adverse effects. A

Tocolytic drugs should be considered for women in PTL as their use may prolong pregnancy for 2 to 7 days, which can allow for administration of steroids to improve fetal lung maturity and the consideration of maternal transport to a tertiary care facility. A

A single dose of antenatal corticosteroids should be given to women at risk of preterm birth. A A repeat dose of prenatal corticosteroids for women still at risk of preterm birth seven days or more after an initial course is associated with less respiratory distress and fewer serious health problems in the first few weeks after birth. A
Antibiotics do not appear to prolong gestation and should be reserved for GBS prophylaxis in patients for whom delivery is imminent. A

Consideration should be given to antenatal magnesium sulphate administration for fetal neuroprotection for women with imminent preterm birth at 24 to and 29 + 6 weeks of pregnancy, with consideration in women between 30 and 33 + 6 weeks although supporting data are limited. B
Neither maintenance treatment with tocolytic drugs nor repeated acute tocolysis improve perinatal outcome; neither should be undertaken as a general practice. A
Bed rest, hydration and pelvic rest do not appear to reduce the rate of preterm birth and should not be routinely recommended. B

The primary aims of tocolytic therapy are to delay delivery to allow the administration of a complete course of antepartum glucocorticosteroid to reduce the incidence and severity of idiopathic respiratory distress syndrome and to arrange in utero transfer to a center with neonatal intensive care unit facilities. The secondary aim of tocolytic therapy is to delay delivery to reduce the perinatal mortality and morbidity associated with severe prematurity.

Tocolytic agents appear useful even in women in PTL with advanced cervical dilation (4-6 cm). Authors of one RCT comparing different tocolytic agents reported that women gained an average of 11.7 days and 60.8% remained undelivered at 48 h regardless of the tocolytic agent used.

Authors of a meta-analysis of RCTs found that prostaglandin-inhibitors such as indomethacin, sulindac and celecoxib and calcium channel blockers (CCBs) were the best choice for the outcomes of 48-hour delay in delivery, respiratory distress syndrome, neonatal mortality, and maternal side effects.

Beta-mimetics (e.g., terbutaline 2.5-5.0 mg every 4 hours) decrease the number of women who will deliver within 48 hours and the number of births within 7 days, but do not reduce rates of preterm birthsperinatal death, neonatal death, or respiratory distress syndrome. There are no data to support use of a particular agent. Beta-mimetics have significant side effects including chest pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, and maternal and fetal tachycardia; they are also associated with pulmonary edema when accompanied by aggressive intravenous hydration.

CCBs (e.g., nifedipine loading dose 10-20 mg sublingual every 20 minutes x3 followed by 10-20 mg every 6 hours) were found to be more effective than beta-mimetics in reducing delivery within 7 days and prior to 34 weeks gestation but there were no differences in perinatal mortality. There was evidence of reduced serious neonatal morbidity and maternal adverse effects.
Nicorandil, a potassium channel opener was comparable to nifedipine for prolongation of pregnancy but associated with more side effects in one small RCT.
In a small RCT, nifedipine as a single tocolytic agent was as effective as combination nifedipine and salbutamol in the delay of preterm births and had fewer side effects.

In an RCT of 239 women with singleton gestations presenting in preterm labor at 24 to 34 weeks' gestation, those randomized to nifedipine plus sildenafil were less likely to have a preterm birth compared to nifedipine alone with fewer deliveries within 7 days of admission (9.1% vs. 20.3%) and fewer deliveries within 7 days of admission (20.7% vs. 38.1%). There were no differences in adverse events between groups.

Combined indomethacin and nifedipine were better than monotherapy with either drug in inhibiting contractions for 7 days (72.2%, 77.7% vs. 90.2%, respectively) and reducing rates of preterm birth (75% delivered prior to 37 weeks for either monotherapy vs. 41.5%) in an RCT of 150 women in PTL at 26 to 34 weeks gestation.

Atosiban, an oxytoxin receptor antagonist, was not found to be superior to placebo, beta-mimetics, or CCBs with respect to pregnancy prolongation or neonatal outcomes; further one trial found an increase in infant deaths with use of atosiban. This result should be viewed with caution and additional study is needed.

In the most recent RCT of 510 women in threatened PTL, perinatal outcomes were similar between atosiban and nifedipine. However, authors of a cost-effectiveness analysis of data from the APOSTEL III Trial concluded that nifedipine was more cost effective than atosiban primarily due to a lower neonatal intensive care unit admission rate.

Prostaglandin inhibitors: Indomethacin (loading dose 50 mg oral or 50-100 mg rectal followed by 25-50 mg orally every 4-6 hours) is effective in delaying PTL; however, potential fetal side effects include premature closure of the ductus arteriosus, necrotizing enterocolitis, oligohydramnios, respiratory distress syndrome and bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

There is insufficient information to assess the potential role of cyclo-oxygenase (COX) inhibitors or nitric oxide donors (e.g., nitroglycerin; 12 trials) on inhibiting PTL. The meta-analysis noted above, however, identified several favorable trials with COX inhibitors.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 31 RCTs of women at high risk for preeclampsia found low-dose aspirin-dipyridamole superior to placebo-no treatment in reducing rates of preterm birth at <37 weeks (RR 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.996); benefit was not apparent for nulliparous women on subgroup analysis.

Preterm premature rupture of membranes; however, in the absence of maternal infection, tocolytics may be considered for the purposes of maternal transport, steroid administration or both. In a matched comparison of 92 women with threatened preterm birth and ruptured membranes, use of tocolysis did not result in statistically significant differences in neonatal composite outcome (9.6% vs. 18% in the control group, OR 0.46, 95% CI, 0.13-1.63).
Maternal contraindications to tocolysis (agent specific)

Magnesium sulfate given to women at risk of preterm birth may have a neuroprotective role for the preterm fetus (NNT = 63 to prevent one case of cerebral palsy [CP]). Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with 5917 women found magnesium sulfate intervention in women at imminent risk for preterm birth decreased the offspring's CP risk (meta-analysis RR 0.68; 95% CI, 0.54-0.85; trial sequential analysis RR 0.69; 95% CI, 0.48-0.97).

The Maternal Fetal Medicine Committee of the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) recommend consideration of antenatal magnesium sulphate administration (4 g intravenous loading dose over 30 minutes followed by a 1 g/h maintenance infusion until birth) for fetal neuroprotection for women with imminent preterm birth (≤31 + 6 weeks); if given, tocolysis should be discontinued.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs and 5 cohort studies confirmed a significant reduction in the rate of moderate to severe CP with antenatal administration of magnesium sulfate to women at high-risk of preterm labor (OR 0.61; 95% CI, 0.42-0.89). There were no other benefits or neonatal adverse effects but many mothers experienced side effects.

Authors of another meta-analysis found no differences in a composite outcome of infant death or CP or in the single outcome of infant death based on 5 RCT’s; using only 4 RCTs, however, showed a modest reduction in the combined outcome (15% vs. 17%; NNT = 43) and in incidence of CP (5% vs. 7%; NNT = 48).

In the most recent placebo-controlled RCT of 560 pregnant women at risk for preterm birth, those randomized to magnesium sulfate had a 1.3% absolute risk reduction of moderate to severe CP (2% vs. 3.3%, respectively).

Closer proximity of magnesium infusion may confer greater benefit as shown in a secondary analysis of a multicenter trial; the authors demonstrated lower rates of CP among the 468 infants exposed at <12 hours prior to delivery compared to the 338 exposed at ≥12 hours prior to delivery (2.3% vs. 4.4%, respectively).

A slower rate of infusion of the magnesium sulphate loading dose over 60 minutes did not reduce the occurrence of maternal adverse effects overall, which occurred in 71% of women. Flushing and warmth at 20 minutes into the infusion was reduced with the slower infusion but there were no differences in stopping treatment.

Magnesium sulfate is ineffective at delaying birth or preventing spontaneous preterm birth after PTL and its use may be associated with an increased risk of total fetal, neonatal or infant mortality. There is insufficient evidence to determine potential benefit from magnesium maintenance therapy after threatened PTL.

strong.em: Steroids for acceleration of fetal lung maturity

list.listitem: A single dose of antenatal steroids should be given to women at risk of preterm birth from 24 + 0/7 to 34 + 6/7 weeks' gestation to accelerate fetal lung maturation; this treatment is associated with an overall reduction in neonatal death (RR 0.78; 95% CI, 0.70-0.87; 2.6% fewer deaths; 22 studies with high-certainty evidence), perinatal death (RR 0.85; 95% CI, 0.77-0.93; 2.3% fewer deaths; 14 studies with high-certainty evidence), and respiratory distress syndrome, and probably cerebroventricular hemorrhage and developmental delay.

In a systematic review of 17 studies of corticosteroid administration vs. placebo or no treatment in neonates born before 24 weeks of gestation, the adjusted odds of mortality to discharge were reduced in the antenatal corticosteroid group vs. the control group (adjusted OR 0.48; 95% CI, 0.38-0.61).

In an RCT of 1427 women at high-risk of late preterm delivery, those randomized to two injections of betamethasone vs. matching placebo 24 hours apart had a reduced rate of a composite of neonatal respiratory support, stillbirth or neonatal death within 72 hours after delivery (11.6% vs. 14.4% for placebo) as well as lower rates of neonatal respiratory complications. There were no significant differences between groups in the incidence of chorioamnionitis or neonatal sepsis, but neonatal hypoglycemia was more common in the betamethasone group (24.0% vs. 15.0%).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 RCTs found use of betamethasone for late PTL at 34 to 36.6 weeks gestation reduced the incidence of transient tachypnea of the newborn (RR 0.56; 95% CI, 0.37-0.86) and severe respiratory distress syndrome (RR 0.55; 95% CI, 0.33-0.91).
Adding thyrotropin-releasing hormones to prenatal corticosteroids does not confer additional benefit and can cause maternal side-effects.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 11 trials including 2494 women at increased risk of preterm birth or who had a medical indication for preterm birth and 2762 infants were unable to find important differences between dexamethasone and betamethasone, or between one regimen and another for accelerating fetal lung maturity.
See below for repeat dosing of prenatal corticosteroids.

A single large RCT did not find antibiotics useful for women in PTL with intact membranes and no clinical signs of infection.ACOG suggests reserving antibiotics for women needing group B streptococcal (GBS) prophylaxis when delivery is imminent.
Data are conflicting regarding the benefits of progestins. For information on progestin use for high-risk women, see secondary prevention.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 7 trials found some evidence of benefit of progestational agents for reducing preterm delivery at <37 weeks, attenuating the shortening of cervical length, and reducing the frequency of uterine contractions. Data are insufficient for recommending their use as tocolytic agents.
A single injection of 17 alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate was ineffective in conjunction with tocolysis and steroids in delaying delivery.

Vaginal progesterone after tocolysis in an RCT of 190 women with threatened PTL resulted in a significant increase in prolongation of pregnancy (7.6 weeks vs. 6.3 weeks). Among women presenting after 27 weeks' gestation, the use of progesterone was associated with a significant reduction in delivery before 34 weeks (9.8% vs. 35.3%) and neonatal birth weight <1500 g (3.2% vs. 20.6%).

In an RCT of 385 women in PTL who were treated with tocolysis, however, those randomized to daily administration of 200 mg vaginal progesterone had similar outcomes to women on placebo for preterm birth and neonatal outcome.

In a systematic review of 16 RCTs with 1,917 women, preterm delivery at <37 weeks was decreased with use of progesterone in women with arrested preterm labor (38.2% vs. 44.3%; RR 0.79; 95% CI, 0.65-0.97), but this difference was no longer observed when only the 5 high-quality trials were included (37.2% vs. 36.9%).

strong.em: Tocolytics are of no benefit for maintenance therapy

list.listitem: Based on 13 RCTs, there is no benefit of beta-mimetics for maintenance therapy after threatened PTL. The two trials on terbutaline pump maintenance therapy (one vs. saline placebo pump and one vs. oral terbutaline) were also negative and did not demonstrate decreased risk of preterm birth.
One study, however, found use of continuous subcutaneous terbutaline effective in preventing preterm birth for women with recurrent PTL.
Based on 6 trials, there was no benefit of nifedipine maintenance therapy with respect to preterm birth rate or improvement in maternal or neonatal outcomes compared with placebo or no treatment.

In a multicenter RCT of 406 women, nifedipine-maintained tocolysis for 12 days did not result in a statistically significant reduction in adverse perinatal outcomes vs. placebo. In this study, investigators enrolled women with threatened PTL between 26 and 32 weeks gestation who had not delivered after 48 hours of tocolysis and had completed a course of corticosteroids.
Maintenance therapy with atosiban vs. placebo also does not confer benefit for reducing preterm birth; rates of neonatal morbidity and perinatal mortality were similar.

listitem.strong: Progesterone use in women with a shortened cervix is of no benefit.

list.listitem: In a high-quality RCT of 265 women with singleton pregnancies and cervical length of <25 mm whose preterm labor was successfully arrested with tocolytics, there was no benefit of vaginal progesterone for maintenance tocolysis. Rates of preterm delivery at <34 weeks' gestation were 7.1% (9/126) vs. 7.6% in the placebo group and 28.6% vs. 22% in the placebo group for delivery at <37 weeks' gestation.

In the most recent RCT of 254 women with singleton pregnancies between 22 and 31 6/7 weeks' gestation and a cervical length of 25 mm or less following arrest of preterm labor with nifedipine or atosiban, use of either weekly intramuscular 17 alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate or daily vaginal progesterone did not reduce preterm birth compared to control women; preterm birth occurred in 23%, 38% and 22%, respectively).
Vaginal progesterone does not appear effective for maintenance tocolysis. B

Repeat dose(s) of prenatal corticosteroids given to women still at risk of preterm birth seven days or more after an initial course reduces the occurrence and severity of neonatal lung disease (NNT = 16, 95%CI 11-29) and serious morbidity (NNT = 39, 95%CI 24-158). A 2-year follow-up study of an RCT of repeat prenatal corticosteroid therapy for 1069 women vs. single steroid treatment followed by placebo for 1035 women, however, did not find differences in death or neurologic impairment at 18 to 24 months of age.

ACOG recommends a repeat dose in women who are <34 weeks gestation and at risk of preterm delivery within the next 7 days, and whose prior course of antenatal corticosteroids was administered more than 14 days previously or as early as 7 days from the prior dose, if indicated by the clinical scenario.

Exposure to repeat doses of antenatal betamethasone vs. a single dose does not increase risk factors for cardiometabolic disease at early school age. In a RCT of 1059 eligible long-term survivors, repeat dose(s) of antenatal corticosteroids was not associated with either benefit or harm in mid-childhood for neurobehavioral or other outcomes.

Prophylactic cervical cerclage vs. no cerclage was examined in 4 trials for women at low and medium risk of mid-trimester loss; it did not reduce overall pregnancy loss or preterm delivery rates. The authors concluded that the role of cervical cerclage remains uncertain for women with a short cervix documented on ultrasound, but two trials failed to show benefit.

In an RCT of 100 women in early PTL, combination emergency cervical cerclage PLUS progesterone was more effective than progesterone alone with respect to pregnancy prolongation (28.44 ± 12.73 days vs. 9.96 ± 3.27) and early neonatal deaths (18% vs. 46%) among other findings.
In a small underpowered RCT, there appeared to be no advantage of retaining a cerclage after preterm premature rupture of membranes and a possibility of increased infection.

In women with twin pregnancy, authors of a meta-analysis of 15 studies representing 726 patients treated with cervical cerclage and 8578 non-cerclage treatment controls found that when the cervical length was <15 mm, the risk ratio of preterm birth at <37 weeks (RR = 0.77) was significantly lower in the cerclage group vs. the non-cerclage group.
Fish oil supplementation reduces the risk of recurrent preterm delivery. However, it did not reduce the risk of complications from preterm delivery.
Vitamin E and C do not reduce risk of preterm delivery.
Probiotics appear to reduce the risk of vaginal infections but there is insufficient evidence to determine whether they are associated with reduced risk of preterm birth.
Bed rest, hydration and pelvic rest do not appear to reduce the rate of preterm birth and should not be routinely recommended.

The World Health Organization (2015) provisionally recommend against routine delivery by cesarean section (CS) for the purpose of improving preterm newborn outcomes, regardless of cephalic or breech presentation based on low-quality evidence.

In a database study of 591 infants who delivered between 23 weeks 0 day and 36 weeks 6 days, no differences in neonatal outcomes were observed between the 368 delivered vaginally and the 223 delivered by CS when adjusting for gestational age, maternal ethnicity, and parity. There were no differences in mean age at delivery or administration of antenatal steroids, but infants delivered by CS were more likely to very preterm, in breech presentation or twins. Complication rates were higher among those delivered by CS vs. vaginally (31.4% vs. 15.5%, respectively).

Authors of a retrospective study of 1320 singelton preterm births of which 26.5% of infants were delivered vaginally found a benefit on APGAR score of CS in appropriate-for-gestational age preterm infants until 28 weeks of gestation and in small-for-gestational age preterm infants until 31 weeks of gestation.

Cesarean delivery of extremely preterm infants <26 weeks gestation increases risk of severe maternal morbidity (defined within each study) compared to cesarean delivery of infants between 26 and 34 weeks (17.6% [607 women at <26 weeks] vs. 10.6% [4,483 women at 26-34 weeks]; RR 1.65; 95% CI, 1.52-1.78; I2 = 40%) based on 6 studies involving 45,572 women.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 primarily observational studies with 12,335 breech infants between 23 + 0 and 27 + 6 weeks with planned active resuscitation concluded that delivery by CS reduced odds of death (OR 0.59; 95% CI, 0.36-0.95, NNT 8) and severe intraventricular hemorrhage (OR 0.51; 95% CI, 0.29-0.91, NNT 12).

Delayed cord clamping (32 ± 16 seconds) vs. immediate cord clamping (6.6 ± 6 seconds) did not result in differences in incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage or late onset sepsis in preterm infants but improved motor function at 18 to 22 months corrected age in one RCT.
Tocolytics are indicated for 48 hours to provide time for glucocorticoids to be given and for transfer to a tertiary facility, if needed.
Maternal transfer to a hospital with neonatal intensive care services should be arranged, if possible, for women with anticipated preterm delivery.

In an RCT of 1,838 women with PPROM at 34 weeks' to 36 6/7 weeks' gestation not in labor, infants born to women randomized to an immediate delivery group compared to an expectant management group had increased incidence of respiratory distress (RR 1.6; 1.1-2.3) and mechanical ventilation (RR 1.4; 1.0-1.8), and spent more time in the neonatal intensive care unit (median 4 days vs. 2 days). Mothers in the expectant management group had higher risks of antepartum or intrapartum hemorrhage, intrapartum fever, use of postpartum antibiotics, and longer hospital stay. There was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of neonatal sepsis.

Similar lack of influence of immediate vs. expectant management on short-term neonatal outcomes was demonstrated among women with late preterm premature rupture of membranes in the PPROMEXIL trial. At 2-year follow-up of 59% of the children born during this trial, however, there were fewer neurodevelopmental difficulties documented on the Ages and Stages Questionnaire in the immediate delivery group compared to expectant management group (16/121 children or 14% vs. 27/113 children or 26%). There were no differences between groups in reported behavioral problems (13% vs. 15%, respectively).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 12 trials with 3617 women and 3628 babies found no clinically important difference in neonatal sepsis between women delivered immediately vs. those managed expectantly following PPROM prior to 37 weeks' gestation. Early birth was associated with increased incidence of neonatal RDS, need for ventilation, neonatal mortality, endometritis, admission to neonatal intensive care, and the likelihood of birth by caesarean section, but a decreased incidence of chorioamnionitis. ACOG offers guidelines based on consensus and expert opinion on management of PPROM.
For women with spontaneous preterm premature rupture of fetal membranes, amniopatch led to complete sealing of the defect in a few women (6/50) with resulting increase in amniotic fluid index.
In a cohort study, 27% of women with singleton pregnancies and 62% of women with twins who presented with suspected PTL delivered preterm. B

Based on a birth registry from Norway, girls born very prematurely (22-27 weeks gestation) have an increased risk of early childhood death and are more likely to deliver preterm offspring; boys born preterm (22-32 weeks) have increased early and late childhood mortality. B
Overall survival for infants born between 20 and 25 weeks' gestation is about 40% and of those who survive to 30 months, morbidity is common (e.g., cerebral palsy in 19%). B

Late preterm births (34 0/7-36 6/7 weeks) compared with term births are associated with increased risk of respiratory distress syndrome and other respiratory morbidity; even at 37 weeks' gestation, odds of respiratory distress syndrome vs. 39 to 40 weeks is increased (adjusted OR 3.1; 95% CI, 2.5-3.7).

In a cohort follow-up study of 1771 singletons and twins delivering at 23.0 to 33.9 weeks' gestation, approximately 1 in 4 had neurodevelopmental impairment at age 2 years. Neonatal morbidities including culture-proven sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis, retinopathy of prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and intraventricular hemorrhage increased the odds of impairment but combinations of these morbidities did not add to the prediction of impairment.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 23 studies found that preterm birth and/or low birthweight were associated with lower educational qualifications, decreased rate of employment, and an increased rate of receipt of social benefits in adulthood.
Preterm survivors have elevated blood pressure and impaired renal function (lower glomerular filtration rate but not increased creatinine) compared to full-term-born controls.
The prevalence of problem feeding is high among preterm-born children at 42% in a meta-analysis of 22 studies including 4381 infants up to 48 months.

cell.label: Patient presents with regular preterm (<37 weeks) contractions, vaginal bleeding, preterm premature rupture of membranes, cramping, low back pain, pelvic pressure, or change in vaginal discharge.

Assess fetal well-being (e.g., non-stress test); if abnormal, consult. Monitor for uterine contractions. Perform urinalysis and treat if positive. Perform sterile speculum examination for pooling, cervical smear for wet prep and culture (trichomonas, gonorrhea, chlamydia, bacterial vaginosis, and GBS), fetal fibronectin and for dilation of cervix. Do digital cervical check once rupture of membranes has been ruled out.
Monitor contractions; recheck cervix in 2 hours. If positive wet prep; treat infection. Progressive cervical change?
Consider cervical ultrasonography; cervical length >30 mm?
Follow up per routine or sooner if recurrent contractions.

Follow up in 1 week or sooner if recurrent contractions. May give progesterone (250 mg IM weekly or 200 mg vaginally, daily) if <37 weeks for patients with history of prior preterm delivery, especially with a short cervix (<15 mm at 22-26 weeks gestation). Consider cervical ultrasonography.

Begin tocolytic agent (beta-mimetic or calcium channel blocker); treat for 48 hours (in order to complete steroid series). Give corticosteroids (betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours for 2 doses or dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses). Do not give repeated doses. Begin antibiotics for group B streptococcal (GBS) prophylaxis. If imminent delivery, consider antenatal magnesium sulphate administration for women =31 + 6 weeks' gestation.
